title: Calibration & Traceability to Reference Standards

references.label: General microbiology/quantitative methods references (ASM, FDA BAM, CLSI)

summary: The practice of periodically checking and adjusting an instrument's readings against a known reference standard, and documenting an unbroken chain connecting that reference standard back to a recognized higher-level standard, so a measurement can be trusted to mean what it claims to mean.
explanation: An uncalibrated instrument can drift over time — a balance that reads slightly heavy, a pipette that delivers slightly less than its dial setting — and without periodic calibration against a known reference, that drift is invisible until it produces an obviously wrong result. Traceability extends this idea: the reference standard used for calibration should itself be certified against a higher-level standard (ultimately tracing back to a national or international metrology standard), documented through an unbroken chain, so that a measurement made in one lab can be meaningfully compared to a measurement made in a different lab using a different instrument.

comparison.example: Checking a balance's readings against a certified calibration weight and adjusting if it has drifted
That calibration weight itself carries a certificate tracing its certified mass back to a recognized national metrology standard

commonMisconceptions: Assuming an instrument that 'seems to be working fine' does not need scheduled calibration checks — drift is often too gradual to notice without a reference comparison.
Using an uncertified or expired reference standard for calibration, which breaks the traceability chain even if the calibration procedure itself was followed correctly.
